symptoms: Concentric ring brown or black spots on older lower leaves ('bullseye' pattern)
Yellow halos surrounding brown leaf lesions
Premature defoliation leaving fruit vulnerable to sunscald
Dark, sunken leathery lesions on stems and fruit stem-ends
causes: High humidity (>80%) and temperatures between 24°C and 29°C
Fungal spores overwintering in infected plant debris and soil
Spreading via splash irrigation, wind-blown rain, or contaminated tools
management: Apply copper-based fungicides or chlorothalonil at first sign of spots
Apply bio-fungicides containing Bacillus subtilis as organic control
Remove and destroy lower infected leaves promptly
prevention: Practice 3 to 4 year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops (e.g. corn, beans)
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers to keep leaves dry
Mulch soil around base of plants to prevent soil splash onto leaves
Space plants adequately (60cm apart) to ensure good air circulation
precautions: Consult local agricultural extension office if leaf yellowing exceeds 30% of plant foliage.
source: ICAR - Indian Agricultural Research Institute & USDA Extension Service

symptoms: Water-soaked dark green to purplish-black lesions on leaf tips and margins
White cottony fungal mold growth on the undersides of leaves in damp weather
Rapid wilting, browning, and collapse of entire vine branches
Firm, brown, leathery rot on tomato fruits
causes: Cool, wet weather with high humidity (>90%) and temperatures 15°C - 22°C
Windborne sporangia travelling miles from infected potato or tomato fields
management: Apply systemic fungicides like Mancozeb, Metalaxyl, or Cymoxanil immediately
Prune affected branches immediately and burn or bury infected plant material (do not compost)
prevention: Plant certified disease-resistant tomato cultivars (e.g., Mountain Magic, Defiant)
Avoid planting tomatoes near potatoes
Apply protective copper fungicides prior to rainy periods during cool weather
precautions: Late Blight spreads rapidly across whole regions. Report outbreaks to agricultural authorities.
source: FAO Agricultural Knowledge Network & State Agricultural University Extension

symptoms: Severe stunting of young tomato plants
Upward curling and cupping of leaf margins
Yellowing (chlorosis) between leaf veins
Drastic reduction in fruit setting and small, flower-dropping plants
causes: Transmitted by Silverleaf Whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) vector
Not transmitted by seeds or mechanical contact
management: Control whitefly populations using yellow sticky traps and neem oil spray (2-3%)
Apply insecticidal soaps or imidacloprid / acetamiprid for heavy vector infestations
Remove virus-infected plants to prevent whiteflies from acquiring and spreading the virus
prevention: Use insect-proof mesh netting (50-mesh) over nursery seedlings
Plant TYLCV-resistant varieties
Reflective silver mulches to repel whiteflies from young plants
precautions: Early protection during seedling stage is essential as young infected plants yield zero marketable fruit.
source: World Vegetable Center & Agricultural University Advisory

symptoms: Small dark brown target-like spots with concentric rings on older leaves
Yellowing around lesions leading to premature leaf drop
Sunken dark brown spots on potato tubers with corky dry rot underneath
causes: Alternating dry and wet weather conditions
Nitrogen-deficient or stressed potato plants are more susceptible
management: Spray mancozeb, azoxystrobin, or difenoconazole according to recommended dosage
Maintain adequate soil nitrogen and potassium levels through balanced fertilization
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed tubers
Practice minimum 3-year crop rotation
Destroy infected crop residue after harvest
precautions: Ensure tubers are fully mature before harvest to prevent skin wounding and tuber infection.
source: Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI) & USDA ARS

symptoms: Large dark brown/black leaf lesions with pale green yellow borders
White mildew fuzz under infected leaves during high moisture mornings
Reddish-brown dry rot extending into potato tuber flesh
causes: High relative humidity (>90%) and leaf wetness for more than 10 hours
Temperatures between 12°C and 24°C
management: Spray systemic contact fungicides like Ridomil Gold or Cymoxanil
Destroy potato vines 2 weeks before harvest (desiccation) to prevent tuber contamination
prevention: Plant resistant cultivars (e.g. Kufri Girdhari, Kufri Karan)
Hill up soil high around plant bases to shield tubers from spores washing down
precautions: Do not harvest in wet weather when spores are actively floating in soil moisture.
source: CPRI Potato Disease Handbook

symptoms: Low crop yield, nutrient chlorosis, poor root penetration, waterlogging
causes: Improper soil pH, over-irrigation, lack of organic matter, monoculture
management: Perform soil testing annually to balance N-P-K ratios and micronutrients (Zinc, Boron)
Apply composted farmyard manure (FYM) or vermicompost at 10-15 tonnes per hectare
Adopt drip irrigation or fertigation to minimize water waste and leaf moisture
prevention: Rotate crops annually with nitrogen-fixing legumes (e.g., chickpea, soybean)
Maintain soil organic carbon above 0.75%
Adopt Integrated Pest Management (IPM) combining biological control and threshold spraying
precautions: Always wear protective gear when handling agricultural sprays and observe harvest wait periods.
source: Department of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare Extension Guidelines

symptoms: Small dark water-soaked leaf spots
Raised dark spots on fruit
causes: Bacteria spread by infected seed, transplants, rain splash, and wet handling
management: Remove severely affected plants and avoid working plants when foliage is wet
Use locally registered products only when recommended by an extension specialist
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and transplants
Use drip irrigation and rotate away from solanaceous crops
precautions: Follow local labels and extension guidance for any plant-protection product.
source: University of Minnesota Extension, Tomato diseases: https://extension.umn.edu/disease-management/tomato-diseases

symptoms: Disease pressure increases when foliage remains wet
Uneven growth can follow irregular soil moisture
causes: Overhead irrigation wets foliage
Large swings between dry and saturated soil
management: Irrigate the root zone when soil moisture requires it rather than on a fixed calendar
Use mulch to reduce evaporation and soil splash
prevention: Prefer drip or furrow irrigation where appropriate
Irrigate early enough for foliage to dry and avoid unnecessary leaf wetness
precautions: Adjust timing and amount to soil type, weather, crop stage, and local extension recommendations.
source: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, Tomato production: https://ipm.ucanr.edu/agriculture/tomato/

symptoms: Leaf curling or yellowing
Sticky honeydew and sooty mold
Visible insects on leaf undersides
causes: Pest populations increase with susceptible plants and excess nitrogen growth
management: Scout leaf undersides and use thresholds recommended locally
Conserve beneficial insects and remove heavily infested plant parts
prevention: Use insect exclusion for young plants where practical
Control weeds that can host pests and avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum sprays
precautions: Identify the pest before treatment and follow local label, re-entry, and harvest restrictions.
source: UC Integrated Pest Management, Tomato pests: https://ipm.ucanr.edu/agriculture/tomato/

symptoms: Poor emergence or misshapen tubers
Scab risk can increase in suitable soil conditions
causes: Compacted, poorly drained, or unsuitable-pH soil
management: Prepare a loose, well-drained seedbed and test soil before amendments
Use soil-test results to guide nutrient applications
prevention: Avoid planting in compacted or waterlogged areas
Maintain organic matter and rotate crops
precautions: Do not apply lime or fertilizer without a soil test and local recommendation.
source: Penn State Extension, Potato production: https://extension.psu.edu/potato-production

symptoms: Cracking, poor tuber development, or irregular size
Disease risk after prolonged wet foliage
causes: Uneven soil moisture during tuber initiation and bulking
management: Maintain relatively even root-zone moisture and monitor soil moisture by field conditions
Reduce irrigation as vines mature according to local production guidance
prevention: Use irrigation methods that limit foliage wetness
Ensure drainage before planting
precautions: Irrigation needs vary with soil, weather, cultivar, and growth stage.
source: University of Maine Cooperative Extension, Potato production: https://extension.umaine.edu/publications/2412e/

disease: Potato Aphid and Colorado Potato Beetle IPM
symptoms: Leaf chewing and defoliation
Curled leaves or honeydew from aphids
causes: Pest adults, larvae, and vectors colonizing potato foliage
management: Scout plants and identify life stages before action
Use crop rotation and conserve natural enemies
prevention: Remove volunteer potatoes and manage weeds
Use resistant or less susceptible cultivars when available locally
precautions: Use only locally registered products and rotate modes of action when treatment is justified.
source: University of Minnesota Extension, Potato insects: https://extension.umn.edu/vegetables/potato

symptoms: Olive-green velvety spots on leaves
Scabby lesions on fruit and premature leaf drop
causes: Spores from infected fallen leaves spread during wet spring weather
management: Remove or shred fallen leaves to reduce inoculum
Use locally timed, registered disease management based on weather and extension alerts
prevention: Plant resistant cultivars where suitable
Maintain canopy air flow through appropriate pruning
precautions: Follow regional apple scab forecasting and product labels.
source: Cornell Cooperative Extension, Apple scab: https://blogs.cornell.edu/fruit/plant-diseases/apple-scab/

disease: Apple Orchard Water and Soil Management
symptoms: Poor shoot growth or fruit size under water stress
Root problems in saturated soil
causes: Insufficient or excessive root-zone water
management: Monitor soil moisture in the root zone and adjust irrigation to tree age and weather
Maintain drainage and avoid standing water
prevention: Use mulch away from the trunk to conserve moisture
Keep irrigation water off foliage when possible
precautions: Use local orchard water-balance recommendations for scheduling.
source: Penn State Extension, Irrigation management in tree fruit: https://extension.psu.edu/irrigation-management-in-tree-fruit

symptoms: Entry holes and frass at the fruit calyx or side
Larval tunnels into the apple core
causes: Codling moth eggs and larvae developing in orchard fruit
management: Use pheromone traps and degree-day or local monitoring information
Remove infested fruit and follow local extension timing
prevention: Sanitize dropped fruit
Use mating-disruption or other IPM tools where locally recommended
precautions: Do not use calendar sprays without scouting or regional pest advisories.
source: UC Integrated Pest Management, Codling moth: https://ipm.ucanr.edu/agriculture/apple-and-pear/codling-moth/

symptoms: White powdery growth on leaves and shoots
Infected berries may crack or fail to develop
causes: Fungus favored by dense canopies and warm conditions
management: Improve canopy exposure with appropriate training and pruning
Use locally registered management based on disease risk and extension guidance
prevention: Plant tolerant cultivars where available
Scout early during susceptible growth stages
precautions: Avoid applying products outside their labeled crop and disease use.
source: UC Integrated Pest Management, Grape powdery mildew: https://ipm.ucanr.edu/agriculture/grape/powdery-mildew/

symptoms: Water stress can reduce shoot and berry development
Dense wet canopies favor disease
causes: Irrigation not matched to vine growth stage and soil water holding capacity
management: Monitor vine and soil water status and schedule irrigation by need
Use trellising and canopy practices that improve air movement
prevention: Prefer methods that deliver water to the root zone
Maintain drainage and avoid prolonged saturation
precautions: Grape water requirements depend on climate, cultivar, soil, and production goals.
source: Oregon State University Extension, Wine grape irrigation: https://extension.oregonstate.edu/catalog/pub/em-9027-irrigation-wine-grapes

symptoms: Fine pale stippling on leaves
Leafhopper nymphs and cast skins on undersides
causes: Leafhoppers feeding on grape foliage
management: Scout foliage and use local thresholds
Conserve predatory insects and manage cover crops appropriately
prevention: Maintain balanced vine vigor
Use targeted interventions only when monitoring shows they are needed
precautions: Confirm pest identity before any treatment.
source: UC Integrated Pest Management, Grape leafhoppers: https://ipm.ucanr.edu/agriculture/grape/leafhoppers/

symptoms: Long gray-green cigar-shaped lesions on leaves
Premature loss of leaf area
causes: Fungal spores spread in humid weather and crop residue
management: Use resistant hybrids where available
Use local disease scouting and extension recommendations
prevention: Rotate crops and manage residue where appropriate
Avoid unnecessary overhead irrigation
precautions: Disease management decisions should reflect hybrid resistance and local risk.
source: Iowa State University Extension, Northern corn leaf blight: https://crops.extension.iastate.edu/encyclopedia/northern-corn-leaf-blight

symptoms: Wilting or poor kernel fill under water stress
Root injury and nutrient loss in waterlogged soil
causes: Water supply not matching crop demand and soil drainage
management: Use soil testing and monitor crop water demand
Maintain drainage and schedule irrigation around sensitive growth stages
prevention: Build soil structure with appropriate residue and organic matter practices
Avoid compaction when soil is wet
precautions: Use local evapotranspiration and soil recommendations for irrigation scheduling.
source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension, Irrigating corn: https://extension.unl.edu/statewide/dodge/irrigating-corn/

symptoms: Silk feeding and damaged kernels near the ear tip
Larvae or frass in ears
causes: Moths lay eggs on silks and larvae enter developing ears
management: Monitor moth activity and silking fields
Use locally recommended biological or chemical controls only when thresholds justify action
prevention: Synchronize planting where appropriate and manage volunteer hosts
Use resistant hybrids if available
precautions: Treatment timing is crop-stage and region specific.
source: University of Minnesota Extension, Corn earworm: https://extension.umn.edu/corn-pest-management/corn-earworm

symptoms: Sudden wilt
Dark lesions on stems and fruit
Root and crown rot
causes: Pathogen survives in soil and spreads in moving water
management: Remove infected plants and improve drainage
Use resistant rootstocks or cultivars where available
prevention: Use raised beds and avoid moving contaminated soil or water
Rotate away from susceptible crops
precautions: Do not move irrigation water from infested to clean fields.
source: Cornell Vegetable Program, Phytophthora capsici: https://blogs.cornell.edu/livegpath/gallery/pepper/phytophthora-blight/

symptoms: Poor growth or nutrient deficiency symptoms
Excess vegetative growth with delayed fruiting
causes: Unbalanced nutrients or unsuitable soil pH
management: Base fertilizer decisions on a soil test
Use balanced fertility and avoid excessive nitrogen
prevention: Incorporate organic matter based on soil conditions
Maintain consistent moisture to reduce blossom-end disorder risk
precautions: Do not diagnose nutrient deficiency from leaf color alone.
source: University of Minnesota Extension, Growing peppers: https://extension.umn.edu/vegetables/growing-peppers

symptoms: Silvery scarring or distorted young leaves
Sticky honeydew and curled leaves
causes: Small insects feed on tender leaves, flowers, and fruit
management: Scout flowers and growing points
Protect beneficial insects and remove heavily infested plant material
prevention: Use clean transplants and manage weeds
Use reflective mulch or exclusion where locally suitable
precautions: Identify the pest and consult local thresholds before treatment.
source: UC Integrated Pest Management, Pepper pests: https://ipm.ucanr.edu/agriculture/pepper/

symptoms: Rapid brown decay on ripening fruit
Tan spore tufts and shriveled mummies
causes: Fungus enters wounded or ripening fruit, especially in wet weather
management: Remove rotted fruit and mummies from trees and orchard floor
Prune to improve air circulation and follow local disease advisories
prevention: Handle fruit carefully to avoid wounds
Maintain sanitation and appropriate canopy openness
precautions: Use only products registered for peach brown rot in the local jurisdiction.
source: Penn State Extension, Brown rot of stone fruits: https://extension.psu.edu/brown-rot-of-stone-fruit

symptoms: Reduced growth under drought stress
Root problems under saturated conditions
causes: Unmanaged soil moisture and competition from weeds
management: Monitor root-zone moisture and irrigate according to tree age and weather
Use organic mulch while keeping it away from the trunk
prevention: Maintain drainage and avoid wetting foliage
Keep a weed-free strip around young trees
precautions: Avoid mulch contact with bark because it can promote trunk problems.
source: University of Georgia Extension, Home garden peaches: https://extension.uga.edu/publications/detail.html?number=C1064

symptoms: Soft brown fruit rot
Gray fuzzy mold on infected fruit
causes: Fungus develops on flowers and fruit during cool, wet conditions
management: Remove diseased fruit and improve air movement
Avoid harvesting or handling when plants are wet
prevention: Use straw or suitable mulch to keep fruit off wet soil
Use drip irrigation and adequate plant spacing
precautions: Follow local resistance-management and label guidance for any fungicide.
source: UMass Extension, Strawberry diseases: https://www.umass.edu/agriculture-food-environment/vegetable/fact-sheets/strawberry-diseases

symptoms: Weak runners and low yield after harvest
Stress from shallow or irregular watering
causes: Crowded beds, depleted soil, and insufficient post-harvest care
management: Renovate established June-bearing beds according to local guidance
Maintain even moisture in the shallow root zone
prevention: Use appropriate spacing and remove excess runners
Test soil and replenish nutrients based on results
precautions: Renovation timing differs by cultivar and production system.
source: Penn State Extension, Strawberry production: https://extension.psu.edu/strawberry-production

symptoms: Small purple spots on leaves
Yellowing and premature defoliation
causes: Spores develop in fallen infected leaves and spread in wet weather
management: Remove or manage fallen leaves and monitor new foliage
Use local extension disease forecasts
prevention: Maintain canopy air movement
Choose tolerant cultivars where available
precautions: Use locally registered products only and follow label restrictions.
source: Michigan State University Extension, Cherry leaf spot: https://www.canr.msu.edu/ipm/diseases/cherry_leaf_spot

symptoms: Maggots in fruit
Small punctures or dark spots on ripening cherries
causes: Adult flies lay eggs in developing fruit
management: Use monitoring traps and local action thresholds
Remove dropped and infested fruit
prevention: Harvest promptly and maintain orchard sanitation
Use exclusion or approved controls where locally suitable
precautions: Follow regional monitoring and pre-harvest interval requirements.
source: Oregon State University Extension, Cherry fruit fly: https://extension.oregonstate.edu/catalog/pub/pnw-626-cherry-fruit-fly

symptoms: Poor growth and small leaves
Wilting despite wet soil
Root browning
causes: Saturated, poorly drained soil favors root infection
management: Improve drainage and avoid planting in waterlogged areas
Remove severely affected plants and use clean planting material
prevention: Build raised beds with suitable acidic media
Use irrigation that maintains moisture without saturation
precautions: Confirm root disease diagnosis before treatment.
source: Oregon State University Extension, Blueberry diseases: https://extension.oregonstate.edu/catalog/pub/pnw-613-blueberry-diseases

symptoms: Chlorosis and weak growth in unsuitable soil
Poor yield from shallow or damaged roots
causes: Blueberries require acidic, well-drained soil and have shallow roots
management: Test soil before planting and use locally recommended amendments
Use organic mulch to conserve moisture and suppress weeds
prevention: Avoid frequent cultivation near roots
Maintain consistent moisture without waterlogging
precautions: Do not acidify soil without a laboratory soil test and extension guidance.
source: University of Maine Cooperative Extension, Growing highbush blueberries: https://extension.umaine.edu/publications/2257e/

symptoms: Dark lesions on canes
Wilting or dieback of fruiting laterals
causes: Wounds and wet conditions allow cane pathogens to enter
management: Prune and destroy infected canes during dry weather
Improve air movement and avoid wounding canes
prevention: Use clean planting stock and trellis canes
Control weeds and avoid overhead irrigation
precautions: Disinfect pruning tools between visibly diseased plants.
source: Penn State Extension, Raspberry diseases: https://extension.psu.edu/raspberry-diseases

symptoms: Small fruit under water stress
Disease pressure in dense, wet rows
causes: Shallow roots, uneven irrigation, and poor canopy ventilation
management: Use drip irrigation and monitor soil moisture
Thin and train canes to maintain row air movement
prevention: Keep rows weed-managed and appropriately spaced
Mulch to conserve moisture without burying crowns
precautions: Spacing and pruning systems depend on cultivar and local climate.
source: Oregon State University Extension, Commercial red raspberry production: https://extension.oregonstate.edu/catalog/pub/pnw-598-commercial-red-raspberry-production

symptoms: Interveinal leaf chlorosis and necrosis
Premature defoliation with infected roots
causes: Soilborne pathogen favored by wet soil and susceptible varieties
management: Use resistant varieties and manage fields with local disease recommendations
Avoid moving infested soil between fields
prevention: Improve drainage where possible
Use crop rotation and certified seed
precautions: Confirm diagnosis because symptoms overlap with other soybean disorders.
source: Iowa State University Extension, Soybean sudden death syndrome: https://crops.extension.iastate.edu/encyclopedia/sudden-death-syndrome

symptoms: Poor vigor or pale plants when biological nitrogen fixation is weak
Uneven growth in compacted soil
causes: Inadequate nodulation, unsuitable pH, compaction, or nutrient imbalance
management: Use soil tests and inspect roots for effective nodules
Correct pH and nutrient issues according to local recommendations
prevention: Use appropriate inoculant on seed where recommended
Avoid compaction and waterlogging
precautions: Do not apply nitrogen routinely without crop and soil diagnosis.
source: University of Minnesota Extension, Soybean nutrient management: https://extension.umn.edu/crop-specific-needs/soybean

symptoms: White powdery colonies on leaves
Premature yellowing and reduced photosynthesis
causes: Mildew fungi spread through air and dense canopies
management: Remove badly affected leaves where practical and improve air movement
Use resistant varieties and local extension recommendations
prevention: Provide suitable spacing and avoid excessive nitrogen
Keep weeds controlled and scout regularly
precautions: Confirm the diagnosis before using a disease-control product.
source: Cornell Vegetable Program, Cucurbit powdery mildew: https://blogs.cornell.edu/livegpath/gallery/cucurbits/powdery-mildew/

disease: Squash Beetle and Vine Borer IPM
symptoms: Leaf feeding and bacterial wilt risk
Sudden vine wilt or sawdust-like frass at the stem base
causes: Cucumber beetles and squash vine borer larvae attack cucurbit plants
management: Scout plants and stems frequently
Remove and destroy infested plant parts where feasible and use row covers before flowering
prevention: Rotate cucurbit fields and remove crop residue
Use resistant or tolerant varieties where available
precautions: Use local thresholds and crop-specific labels for any treatment.
source: University of Minnesota Extension, Squash and pumpkin insects: https://extension.umn.edu/vegetables/growing-squash-and-pumpkins

symptoms: Uneven growth and nutrient deficiency symptoms
Poor root development
causes: Unknown soil fertility, pH, salinity, or compaction
management: Collect a representative soil sample and use a laboratory test
Base lime, sulfur, and fertilizer decisions on test results
prevention: Test before planting and periodically thereafter
Record amendments and crop performance by field
precautions: Soil pH targets differ by crop; use crop-specific extension guidance.
source: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, Soil health: https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/conservation-basics/soil-health

symptoms: Unidentified plant injury or pest presence
causes: Pests, pathogens, environmental stress, or nutrient disorders
management: Identify the cause, monitor population and crop damage, and use action thresholds
Prefer prevention, biological, cultural, and mechanical controls before targeted chemical control
prevention: Scout routinely and keep field records
Protect beneficial organisms and rotate crops when appropriate
precautions: Read and follow the local product label; never infer dosage from general advice.
source: USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture, Integrated Pest Management: https://www.nifa.usda.gov/topics/integrated-pest-management

symptoms: Evaporation, weeds, soil splash, and temperature fluctuations
causes: Bare soil and poorly timed cultivation
management: Use suitable organic or synthetic mulch to conserve water and suppress weeds
Keep mulch away from plant crowns and trunks
prevention: Choose mulch suited to crop and climate
Combine mulching with crop rotation, sanitation, and appropriate spacing
precautions: Avoid contaminated mulch and excessive thickness that restricts aeration.
source: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, Soil health and residue management: https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/conservation-basics/soil-health
